10661-a-selection-from-the-discourses-of:
Epictetus, a Greek slave in Rome who later taught philosophy, speaks in this selection from his Discourses, translated by George Long, with the short manual called the Encheiridion. Born at Hierapolis in Phrygia, he served a freedman of Nero, and tradition says his leg was broken by his master's cruelty. His teaching survived through notes taken by his students.

The discourses urge readers to separate what they can control from what they cannot, and to meet fortune with calm and duty. The Encheiridion compresses that counsel into brief rules for daily life. Readers get a plain, sturdy Stoic guide, short enough to carry and strong enough to return to.
17827-the-story-of-mattie-j-jackson-her-:
Mattie J. Jackson's story, of her parentage, eighteen years in slavery, incidents during the war, and her escape from slavery, was written and arranged by Dr. L. S. Thompson, formerly Mrs. Schuyler, as given by Mattie herself. The true story was printed in Lawrence in 1866 at the Sentinel office. Mattie's own opening recalls ancestors transported from Africa to America when the slave trade flourished in the Eastern States.

She cannot give dates, since her progenitors, being enslaved, kept no records of the kind. Readers get a short, direct slave narrative from the war's aftermath, told in Mattie's voice through Thompson's arrangement. The book suits readers of slave narratives and of emancipation history.
21235-the-maidens-lodge-or-none-of-self-:
The story opens in 1712, in Queen Anne's reign, around a gentle family and two young women, Rhoda and Phoebe. Emily Sarah Holt studies the habits, loves, and hates of minor gentry of the day. Madam Furnival rules her narrow domain like an empress, and dependants would never dare call her Mrs.

A rich-seeming Mr Welles, said to have three thousand pounds a year, courts the girl he thinks will inherit a large estate. A poor curate nearby has twenty-one pounds and a big family. Welles has picked the wrong girl. The latter chapters follow his greedy mistake, his attempts to recover, and his rebuff.
25115-a-journal-of-a-visit-of-three-days:
Elihu Burritt's Journal of a Visit of Three Days to Skibbereen, published in London in 1847, is a firsthand report from the Irish famine at its worst. Burritt, an American peace advocate known on both sides of the Atlantic, visited the distressed districts. He meant to send facts, from his own observation, to readers in the United States.

In Skibbereen and the Castle-haven district he entered hovels and holes in walls where families lay starving. Some had gone without food for a full day, and children slept in straw with staring eyes. Quoting Lord John Russell on the failure of poor rates, Burritt's appeal helped turn distant suffering into a call for American relief.
31848-a-proposal-for-the-better-supplyin:
This 1725 proposal was printed in London by H. Woodfall and sold for sixpence. It argues for better supplying churches in the foreign plantations and for converting the native Americans to Christianity through a college built in the Summer Islands. Those islands are otherwise called the Isles of Bermuda. Its epigraph quotes Luke: the harvest is truly great, but the labourers are few.

The author notes that excellent persons of the Church of England have combined into societies to propagate the gospel in the West Indies and the East. Yet there remains little sense of religion and a notorious corruption of manners in the plantations. Readers get a famous colonial missionary scheme, idealistic and imperial, from the early eighteenth century.
33835-journal-of-voyages-containing-an-a:
Captain Jacob Dunham published this seaman's journal in New York in 1850. Twice taken by the English, once by Gibbs the pirate, chased by a war schooner, and cast away among Native peoples, Dunham lived a life of narrow escapes. He adds notes on the soil, products, laws, and customs of Chagres, the Mosquito Shore, and Saint Blas.

Chapters follow his sloops Rover, New York, and Biddle through capture, exchange of prisoners, and wreck near the Waa-waa River. Dunham writes in a plain sailor's voice, with an eye for trade and shore life. The journal offers a vivid first-hand view of the seas around the Isthmus of Darien.
36457-a-treatise-on-meteorological-instr:
Negretti and Zambra wrote A Treatise on Meteorological Instruments, published in London in 1864. The firm made instruments for the Queen and the Royal Observatory at Greenwich. The subtitle promises their scientific principles, construction, and practical use. The book sold for five shillings.

The preface argues that storm warnings have made weather instruments common tools. Every well-informed person now needs to know how they work. Earlier accounts hid in large scientific works and touched the subject briefly. This volume describes every instrument in use, plainly and in one place. Full directions for using each one are included. Buyers can thus choose the tools that fit their needs. Old and obsolete instruments are mostly passed over. A few earn a place for historical interest alone.
38355-light-and-peace-instructions-for-d:
Padre Quadrupani, a Barnabite priest, wrote Light and Peace to guide devout souls past doubt and fear. He wrote the work in 1795 in his own tongue. The English form here came from the French and was put out at Saint Louis in 1898. P J Ryan, the church head at Philadelphia, wrote the first words.

Quadrupani shaped his rule of life on the life and thought of Francis de Sales. The guide speaks to plain folk who live and work in the world. Its maxims stress calm, good sense, and small steps done with care. The new form was made since the old English one had grown rare and flawed. A calm, kind tone runs through the whole short book.
38501-the-memoirs-of-charles-lewis-baron:
Volume two of The Memoirs of Charles Lewis, Baron de Pollnitz, is a second edition printed in London in 1739. The memoirs take the form of letters to a friend, recording travels from Prussia through Germany, Flanders, Italy, Holland, France, and England. They promise not only the present state of chief cities and towns but the characters of principal persons at the several courts.

Letters twenty eight through fifty four fill this volume, with an index at the end. Letter twenty eight, dated from Rome on July 30, 1730, finds the baron at last in the famous city. He warns his friend not to expect a perfect description, and says he will report things animate rather than inanimate.
38519-the-memoirs-of-charles-lewis-baron:
Volume four of the memoirs of Charles-Lewis, Baron de Pollnitz, was printed at London in 1738 for Daniel Browne and John Brindley. It gathers the observations he made traveling from Prussia through Poland, Germany, Italy, France, Spain, Flanders, Holland, and England. The title page promises the present state of the chief cities and the characters of the principal persons at the several courts.

The volume opens with a letter on the war of 1718. While the Emperor fought the Turks and Prince Eugene won his signal victory near Belgrade, Spain fitted out her most formidable fleet since the Invincible Armada. She landed an army in Sicily under the Marquis de Lede. Admiral Bing brought the English fleet into the Mediterranean with orders to resist if Spain would not desist. Cardinal Alberoni answered that he had nothing to do but put them in execution.
46036-the-sidereal-messenger-of-galileo-:
Edward Stafford Carlos translated The Sidereal Messenger of Galileo Galilei for Rivingtons at London in 1880, with an opening essay and notes. Carlos was head mathematical master at Christ's Hospital. Part of the preface to Kepler's Dioptrics joins the text. A plate shows Galileo's broken lens, kept at South Kensington.

Carlos found his source while cataloguing old books at Christ's Hospital for the Royal Mathematical Foundation. A London volume of 1653 held Gassendi on the rival systems, Galileo's Sidereus Nuncius, and Kepler. The Messenger gives Galileo's own first account of his telescope discoveries. Carlos puts the Latin into English for students who know the name but have never seen the book.
48065-anecdotes-of-the-manners-and-custo:
Anecdotes of the Manners and Customs of London During the Eighteenth Century, by James Peller Malcolm, was printed in London in 1810 in a second edition. Forty five plates fill the book. Malcolm had also written Londinium Redivivum.

Volume one opens with the state of parish children and tales of charity in London from 1700 to 1800. The next part treats tales of vice and crime in the same span. Later parts cover dress, fun, and the daily ways of London folk. Malcolm adds a review of society in 1807 and a sketch of home building in the city. He first meant to trace London habits from the earliest ages. Readers get a rich store of street level past.
48066-anecdotes-of-the-manners-and-custo:
Anecdotes of the Manners and Customs of London, volume two, surveys the city past. James Peller Malcolm wrote it; Longman issued the second edition in 1810. Forty five engravings show dress, houses, and street scenes of old London. A review of society in 1807 crowns the second volume plan here.

Chapter five opens on state lotteries as public money raising in 1709. Tickets at ten pounds each promised nine per cent interest for years. Later chapters treat popular tumults of religious and political passion in town. Amusements since 1700 and the caprices of fashion get long full chapters. Domestic architecture and street improvement close the survey of the metropolis.
54984-a-serious-proposal-to-the-ladies-f:
An anonymous tract signed by a lover of her sex was printed at London in 1697, in two parts, proposing a scheme for women's advancement. Ladies, it opens, profitable adventures abroad have won great encouragement, though their prizes are uncertain lots. Things gained by chance are as flitting and fickle as that chance, the author argues. A proposition with more certain and substantial gain should meet a kinder welcome.

The proposal is famous as an early call for women's education and a female college. Its author writes to improve women's characters, she says, not to chase opinion's prizes. The tract is now credited to Mary Astell. Its two parts argue the scheme and answer objections.
57152-the-three-voyages-of-captain-cook-:
The Three Voyages of Captain Cook Round the World, volume two of seven, continues the official account of Cook's first voyage. Longman and partners printed the set in London in 1821, with a map and other plates. This volume is the second half of the first voyage, in New Zealand and Australian waters.

The contents open with the run from Cape Turnagain southward along the eastern coast of the southern island. Cook rounded Cape South and came back to the western entrance of Cook's Strait, completing the circumnavigation of the country. A description of the coast and of Admiralty Bay follows. Then comes the departure from New Zealand and the run to Botany Bay, on the east coast of New Holland, now called New South Wales. Incidents there, and an account of the country and its inhabitants, close the volume. A New Zealand canoe is pictured.
61050-lorelei:
Charles De Vet wrote Lorelei, a science fiction tale from Worlds of If in September 1961. A castaway named Bill has spent seven days stranded on Europa, without hope of rescue. Courage slips like numbness fading after a fatal blow, and his nerves balance on a thin jagged edge.

On the seventh night an anamorph visits him in his bubble cubicle, rustling in a crinoline skirt with a scent of fragrance. She comes, he knows, to those whose morale is nearest breaking, probing his mind for the face he longs for. She was everyone's sweetheart, the blurb says, but not every man's at once. He fights to resist her soft, warm pull. The tale probes loneliness.
61492-the-three-voyages-of-captain-cook-:
Volume four of The Three Voyages of Captain James Cook Round the World, printed at London in 1821 for Longman and partners, is the second volume of the second voyage. Its first book sails from Ulietea to New Zealand: the Friendly Isles, a robbery at Anamocka and its consequences, and observations on the islanders' sailing canoes and navigation. The passage on discovers Turtle Island and reaches Port Sandwich in Mallicollo, then Tanna, with a skirmish on one island and intercourse established on another.

Later chapters survey the New Hebrides, discover New Caledonia, and describe its country, inhabitants, manners, and arts while the ship lay in Balade. Norfolk Island is discovered on the way back to Queen Charlotte's Sound. The second book runs from New Zealand to Terra del Fuego and Christmas Sound. The seven-volume set carries a map and plates, and the contents list is detailed chapter by chapter.
61575-mahatma-gandhi-the-man-who-became-:
Romain Rolland wrote this life of Gandhi, turned into English by Catherine Groth and printed by the Century Company at New York and London. Mahatma, Rolland explains, means the great soul, a name from the Upanishads for one who has become one with the universal being. The people of India gave the name to Gandhi, and Tagore used it of him.

Rolland draws the man first as witnesses saw him: dark, tranquil eyes, a small frail body in coarse white cloth, bare feet, and a diet of rice, fruit, and water. He sleeps little, works without pause, and meets even opponents with patience and love. A friend who met him in South Africa thought of Saint Francis of Assisi. The book carried Gandhi's fame across the West.
61986-greek-vase-painting-griechische-va:
Greek Vase Painting is an art history by Ernst Buschor, issued at London in 1921. Richards turned the German work into English, and Percy Gardner wrote a preface. One hundred and sixty illustrations carry the argument from plate to plate. The frontispiece shows Theseus with Athena and Amphitrite on a signed kylix cup.

Contents move from the stone and bronze ages through the geometric style of Greece. The seventh century and the black figured style fill the next two chapters. Red figured work of the archaic age and the age of Polygnotos and Pheidias follow. Late offshoots close a compact survey of the Greek painted vase tradition.
62507-the-three-voyages-of-captain-cook-:
The Three Voyages of Captain Cook round the World, volume six, is the second volume of Cook's third voyage, issued at London in 1821. The set ran to seven volumes, complete, with maps and other plates. A plate shows a canoe of the Sandwich Islands, its rowers masked. The contents open with the third voyage's third book.

Dealings at Tahiti and the Society Islands fill the early heads, then the push on to the coast of North America. An eclipse of the moon observed, and an island discovered, open the first chapter. Its situation, extent, and look are described, and its people, their persons, dresses, and canoes. Arrival in a Tahitian bay and the reception of Omai, the islander carried to England and back, follow in the same heads. Cook's own journals, worked up for the press, are the ground of the whole.
67341-traumerei:
Charles Beaumont wrote Traumerei, a tale printed in Infinity Science Fiction in February, nineteen fifty-six, with art by Remington. A head note asks whether the reader has had bad nightmares lately, and warns that after this tale he may fear to dream at all. Henry Ritchie jerks at a buzzer and spills most of his martini over his robe. His wife Ruth slams her book shut in anger.

A large visitor, Max Kaplan, a city editor, lets himself be welcomed with poor grace and drains the martini jar. He looks older than his years, and his grin has lost its boyish air. The clock's tick grows loud in the room as he says less than an hour remains. The tale hangs on what Kaplan knows and why the night will not let the Ritchies rest.
9958-explorations-in-australia-1-explora:
John Forrest, a fellow of the Royal Geographical Society, published these Australian explorations in 1875, with illustrations by G. F. Angas. The volume gathers three journeys: first, the search for Dr. Leichardt and his party, lost in the interior.

Second comes the trek from Perth to Adelaide around the Great Australian Bight, and third, the crossing from Champion Bay over the desert to the telegraph line and Adelaide. An appendix reports the condition of Western Australia. Readers get exploration at its hardest: heat, distance, and the search for water, told by the man who led the way.
a-selection-from-the-discourses-of-epict: Epictetus speaks in this selection from his Discourses with the Encheiridion, translated by George Long. The biographical note traces him to Hierapolis in Phrygia, then to slavery in Rome under Epaphroditus, a freedman of the Emperor Nero. Bodily weak and lame since youth, according to Simplicius, he taught a philosophy of endurance that the Manual distils into short precepts for daily life.
britannica-1911-agnus-dei:
Agnus Dei is the figure of a lamb bearing a cross. It symbolizes the Saviour as the Lamb of God. Ecclesiastical art uses the device commonly. In the Roman Church the name attaches to wax cakes specifically. Easter candle wax forms those small cakes. The lamb figure is impressed upon them. Popes have blessed them since the ninth century. Distribution follows on the Sunday after Easter. The faithful prize them as averting evil.

Music gives the name a second life. Agnus Dei also names an anthem of the mass. Pope Sergius I is said to have introduced it. Its Latin words come from John's gospel. The choir repeats it three times before communion. Many litanies append it as well. An 1890 judgment allowed its English singing in Anglican communion.
britannica-1911-argei:
Argei is the subject of an entry on Roman custom in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. The name was given to a set of rush puppets made to look like men. Counts of the puppets vary by source, from the low twenties to thirty. They were tied hand and foot for the rite.

Each year in May they were carried to an ancient bridge over the Tiber. Priests, magistrates, and Vestal virgins took part in the rite. The puppets were thrown into the river from the bridge. Chapels tied to the rite stood in parts of the city, and a procession visited them in March. Old writers are cited for each detail.
britannica-1911-brunei:
Brunei is a state on the north-west coast of Borneo, once powerful and by this entry's time greatly shrunk. It formerly included the whole of northern Borneo and southern Palawan and stretched down the west coast as far as Sambas. What remains is a triangular territory with 80 miles of coastline for its base and the frontiers of Sarawak for its two sides, about 1700 square miles in all.

Successive cessions of strips of land to Sarawak and to the British North Borneo Company, made for annual money payments, brought about the shrinkage. In 1888 the state was placed under British protection, and by a treaty of 2 January 1906 the sultan agreed to hand general administration to a British resident. Sultan Mahommed Jomal-ul-alam, born in 1889, succeeded his father in May 1906 and receives an allowance of 12,000 dollars a year from state funds, his two chief ministers 6000 dollars each.
britannica-1911-kuroki-itei: Count Itei Kuroki (1844– ) was a Japanese general, born in Satsuma. He made his name in the Chino-Japanese War of 1894–95. In the Russo-Japanese War of 1904–5 he commanded the First Army. He won the first battle of that war at the Yalu river. Then he pushed on through the mountains, and fought beside the other armies at Liao-Yang, Shaho and Mukden. For the earlier war he was made a baron, and for the later one a count.
britannica-1911-liguori-alfonso-maria-de:
Alfonso Maria dei Liguori (1696-1787) was an Italian saint and church teacher. He was born at Marianella near Naples on 27 September 1696. Law was his first trade, with a good practice at the bar. One lost suit, lost through his own misread of a key paper, drove him out of the courts for good.

Orders came in 1726. In 1732 he founded the Congregation of the Most Holy Redeemer at Scala. Its men, called Redemptorists, teach the poor, above all in country parts. His Glories of Mary came in 1750. A great work on moral theology came in 1753 and grew in Latin dress in 1755. A bishop's post at Sant' Agata came in 1762, at the pope's own wish. He gave it up in 1775 and died at Nocera in 1787. Pope Pius IX named him a Doctor of the Church in 1871.
britannica-1911-wei-hai-wei:
Wei-hai-wei was a British sea base and coal post on the north east shore of a cape land in China. It was once a Chinese sea post of strong walls. Japan took it in war in eighteen ninety-five and held it till a fee was paid. Past a foe lands grab of a near port, Britain took a lease of it in eighteen ninety-eight.

The port is formed by an isle that runs past the mouth of a small bay. The leased land holds the port, the isle, and a belt of shore past the bay. Britain held sole rule there and the right to build forts. Some three hundred hamlets and past a vast count of folk lay in that tract.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-agnus-dei:
Agnus Dei names certain wax discs impressed with a lamb's figure, blessed by the pope at stated seasons. Usually the lamb bears a cross or flag. Saints' figures or the pope's name and arms commonly appear on the reverse. By their consecration they count, like holy water and blessed palms, as sacramentals.

Their origin is much obscured. Recent authorities stress the lack of evidence for them before the ninth century. They probably began in some pagan use of charms or amulets, from which this Christian substitute weaned the ruder populace blessed by prayer. It is not disputed that they originated in Rome, perhaps traceable to paganism's final overthrow there, say the fifth century. When first heard of, about 820, they were made from the preceding year's paschal candle remnants. Ennodius about 510 already notes paschal candle fragments used against tempests and blight.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-allesandro-ga:
Alessandro Galilei was an eminent Florentine architect, born in 1691 and dead in 1737. Once he had made some name, several noblemen invited him to travel with them to England, where he lived seven years. He then went back to Tuscany, where the Grand Dukes Cosimo III and Giovanni Gastone made him state architect. He erected nothing remarkable either in England or in Tuscany.

His abilities showed at Rome, where Clement XII had invited him. He designed the façade of St. John of the Florentines in 1734 and the great façade of St. John Lateran, the latter winning among twenty-one designs in a contest Clement XII had launched. He also designed the Corsini chapel in the same church. Critics faulted his arrangement of the orders, but his ornamental treatment wins praise, and he was well versed in mathematics with many other valuable acquirements.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ancilla-dei:
Ancilla Dei, Latin for handmaid of God, appears often in early Christian inscriptions as the title of a dead woman. From its medieval meaning, some assumed, without enough proof, that every woman so styled in the first Christian age was a consecrated virgin. The inscriptions fall into two classes. Some call a woman ancilla Dei. Others make clear the title also went to women who were not religious. The second class settles the question.

One case records a husband raising a monument to his wife, whom he styles Dei ancilla, as Laurentius Rufine coniugi Dei ancillae. A Roman inscription from the sixth century calls Guttes ancilla Dei, yet adds that she was nonnes, a nun. That addition proves the title alone did not mark a religious, since the writer felt he must state her state. From the pontificate of Gregory the Great, from 590 to 604, only nuns bore the title.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-auctorem-fide:
Auctorem Fidei was a bull issued by Pope Pius VI on 28 August 1794. It condemned the Gallican and Jansenist leanings of the Synod of Pistoia of 1786. Its background lay in Tuscany, where Grand Duke Leopold II claimed supreme power over church affairs in his lands, following his brother Joseph II of Austria. In 1785 Leopold sent fifty-seven articles to every bishop in the duchy for debate in diocesan synods.

Scipio de' Ricci, Bishop of Pistoia, approved those articles at his synod and added more of the same stamp. Among them were claims that church authority comes from the members at large. Bishops, they said, need no papal grant of jurisdiction, and parish priests vote on equal terms with bishops. The bull catalogued and condemned the synod's propositions, Ricci at last submitted, and he died repentant at Florence in 1810.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bernardino-ma: Bernardino Maffei, poet, orator, and antiquarian, was born at Bergamo in 1514 and died at Rome in 1549. He studied law at Padua, served as secretary to Cardinal Alessandro Farnese and then to Pope Paul III, and rose to Bishop of Massa Maritima, Archbishop of Chieti, and cardinal in 1549. His commentary on Cicero's letters ranks among the best, and he wrote on ancient coins and inscriptions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-domenico-pass:
Domenico Passionei was a cardinal and theologian born at Fossombrone on 2 December 1682. Schooled at the Clementine College in Rome, he joined his brother's household and pursued higher studies at the Sapienza. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry tells how he was sent to Paris in 1706 to bear the red hat to the nuncio, and there picked up Jansenist leanings he never wholly shook off.

Confidential missions took him to The Hague in 1708 and to Utrecht in 1712, where he upheld the Holy See on religion with success. Baden and Turin went less well. Later he served as inquisitor at Malta, then as Secretary of Propaganda and of Latin Letters. Sorrows late in life hastened his death in 1761, the entry records.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francesco-maf:
Francesco Maffei, born at Vicenza and dead at Padua in 1660. He was an Italian painter whose pleasing pictures still fill churches in Vicenza and towns across Lombardy, though little is known of his life. He studied under Peranda but modelled his work on Veronese, whose opulence of colouring shows in his painting. Unfortunately his work has survived badly, whether from hurried execution or faulty mixing of pigments, a flaw plain in his Paradise in San Francesco at Padua.

His St. Anne at San Michele in Vicenza is probably the best expression of his poetic fancy and colour sense. The entry treats him as a painter of charm and fertility rather than of lasting influence, valued for the many agreeable works he left behind.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-galileo-galil:
Galileo Galilei, born at Pisa in 1564, is remembered by most as an astronomer, yet his deepest mark lies in mechanics. His father, a musician of straitened means, meant him for medicine, but the boy's bent for mathematics and machines won out. Galileo wed experiment to calculation and struck at the habit of learning nature from Aristotle's authority rather than from nature itself.

Before twenty, watching a swinging lamp in Pisa Cathedral, he found the pendulum's equal beats, later used in an astronomical clock. A treatise on centers of gravity won him the name Archimedes of his time and a Pisa lectureship. From the leaning tower he tested falling bodies and disproved the rule that weight sets speed of fall, rousing the fury of the Aristotelians.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-baptist-:
John Baptist Tolomei was a Jesuit theologian and cardinal who mastered eleven languages and taught philosophy and theology at the Roman College. Born near Pistoia in 1653, he studied law at Pisa and entered the Society of Jesus in 1673. He began his public career expounding Scripture in the Church of the Gesu on Sunday evenings. Elected procurator general of the order at thirty, he later took the chair of philosophy at the Roman College.

His lectures, printed in 1696 as Philosophy of Mind and Senses, stayed loyal to Aristotle while welcoming every new discovery of natural science. They won praise from the Leipzig Academy and from Leibniz. He then taught theology and renewed Bellarmine's controversial courses in six folio volumes of manuscript. He served as rector of the Roman and German colleges, and, made cardinal in 1712, advised Clement XI on condemning the errors of Quesnel.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-karl-von-holt:
Karl von Holtei was a German novelist, poet, and dramatist, born at Breslau in 1798 and dead there in 1880. He abandoned agriculture and law for the stage. Marrying actress Louise Rogée, he joined Breslau's theatre, then followed her to Berlin. After her death in 1825 he wandered as a rhapsodist, giving dramatic readings at Paris and elsewhere.

A second marriage in 1829, to actress Julie Holzbecher, preceded stage work in many towns and Riga's German theatre directorship in 1837. His wife's death the next year sent him wandering again until he settled at Graz, returning to Breslau in 1870 in popularity. Failing health took him to the Brothers of Mercy convent, where he died. He introduced the vaudeville into Germany and wrote forty-six plays. Best known are Der alte Feldherr and Lenore of 1829, Ein Trauerspiel in Berlin of 1838, and Lorbeerbaum und Bettelstab of 1840.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-marchese-fran:
Francesco Scipione Maffei was an Italian man of letters and archaeologist, born at Verona in 1675 and dead there in 1755. He came from an old and famed family, once of Bologna. His brother was General Alessandro Maffei, whose Memoirs he published. Early poems suffered from the age's bad taste, but friends and great Italian poets reshaped his style.

In 1699 he joined Rome's Accademia degli Arcadi and set up a Verona branch. He served in the Bavarian army in 1703 and fought at Donauworth in 1704. At Padua he shared editing the Giornale de' Letterati with Apostolo Zeno. Years of digging and collecting filled his palace with antiquities. His Verona histories stirred such thanks that townsfolk wished to raise his statue in his lifetime. His Istoria diplomatica of 1727 advanced the study of charters, and Paris made him a member of its Academy of Inscriptions after four years there.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-promotor-fide:
The Promoter of the Faith is an official of the Roman Congregation of Rites. Clement XI created the office on 7 April 1708.  His chief work lies in beatification and canonization processes, run by the Congregation of Rites.

His special care is to block rash rulings on the miracles or virtues of candidates for the altar's honours. All beatification and canonization papers must pass his eye. The doubts and difficulties he raises over virtues and miracles go ere the congregation and must be met in full ere any step further is taken. He must offer natural readings of alleged miracles, and even human and selfish motives for deeds counted as heroic virtues. For witnesses outside Rome, he frames the questions and may name sub-promoters to aid him. All processes must pass ere the promoter, on pain of nullity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-raffaelo-maff:
Raffaelo Maffei, humanist, historian and theologian, was born on 17 February 1451 and died on 25 January 1522. This encyclopedia entry calls him Raphael Volaterranus, a native of Volterra. From youth he devoted himself to letters. In 1466 his father Gherardo called him to Rome. Pius the Second had made Gherardo professor of law at the University of Rome, then his secretary, a post he kept under Paul the Second and Sixtus the Fourth.

At Rome Raffaelo kept aloof from court life, giving his time to piety and to philosophy, theology and Greek, the last under George of Trebizond. In 1477 he travelled to Hungary with Cardinal Louis of Aragon, on a mission to Matthias Corvinus. On returning, the Blessed Gaspare da Firenze persuaded him not to become a Minor Observant, the entry notes, and his later career unfolded in Rome. Falconcini's life of Maffei supplies the entry's chief source.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-servus-servor:
Servant of the Servants of God is a title popes give themselves in documents of note. This short entry traces it to Gregory the Great, who used it widely as a lesson in humility to John the Faster, Patriarch of Constantinople. Gregory had used the phrase even earlier, while still a deacon, and a bull of 570 already opens with John III calling himself by it.

Successors copied Gregory, though not invariably until the ninth century. Bishops moved by humility, archbishops moved by pride, and even kings and an emperor took the title for themselves at times. Since the twelfth century, the entry notes, it belongs to the pope alone.
doe-osti-3017000-charpy-impact-character:
Mikhail A Sokolov of Oak Ridge National Laboratory wrote report ORNL/SPR-2025/4204 in September 2025 for the Light Water Reactor Sustainability Program. It gives Charpy impact test results for surveillance specimens harvested from the Palisades plant's high fluence A-60 capsule. Charpy tests strike a notched sample and measure how much energy it absorbs. The results show how brittle reactor steel has become after years of radiation.

Four specimen groups rode in the capsule. They were standard reference material, weld metal, base metal, and heat-affected zone metal, with twelve specimens in the groups detailed in the report. Base metal here is A533B-1 plate, a standard reactor vessel steel. Chemistry notes cap the nickel content used in the regulatory chemistry factor at 1.20 weight percent. Plant life-extension teams use exactly this kind of data to judge whether a vessel can keep running safely.
explorations-in-australia-1-explorations:
Forrest's Explorations in Australia collects three journeys across the continent's west and south. John Forrest led the expeditions and wrote the volume, dated 1875. G. F. Angas supplied the illustrations. He dedicates the book to Governor Frederick Weld of Western Australia.

The first part recounts the search for Dr. Leichardt and his party. The second runs from Perth to Adelaide around the Great Australian Bight. The third crosses the desert from Champion Bay to the telegraph line and Adelaide. An appendix reports the condition of Western Australia. Forrest thanks Weld's zeal for reviving colonial exploration. The first chapter surveys earlier attempts to enter the interior. The book is a firsthand record of survey travel.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CommitteeForAct:
The Quarterly Journal of the Fifth Estate was the publication of the Committee for Action and Research on the Intelligence Community, a Washington group that tracked the CIA in print. This file holds volume 2, issue 2, the Winter 1975 issue.

The issue includes a statement from Philip Agee, the former CIA officer whose book had just named the agency's personnel wholesale, and material on CIA chiefs of station around the world. In 1975, with the Church Committee sitting, such a journal was part of the pressure that kept the revelations coming. The issue is preserved as a specimen of the seventies intelligence-watch press.
nasa-tm-19650019885-on-the-evolutionary-:
Richard Stothers, at the Goddard Institute for Space Studies in New York, wrote this paper on Beta Cephei stars. These stars vary in brightness in a regular rhythm. Stothers tries to explain them as stars that do not rotate, but instead swell and shrink in radial oscillations. His attempt rests on their fairly low observed rotation speeds and on period studies by van Hoof.

Arguments from the stars' central conditions form part of his case. The question matters because a star's pulsation reveals its inner state and its stage of life. An evolutionary account must fit both the periods seen and the stars themselves. Stothers offers a careful theory aimed at that fit.
podcast-dannyjones-RmPpOps1yeI:
John Kiriakou is the former CIA officer who confirmed the agency's waterboarding program on television and went to prison for it. He joins Danny Jones to break his silence, as the episode bills it, on Elon Musk's Twitter Files: the internal records Musk released showing government pressure on the platform's moderation decisions.

Kiriakou reads the files with an ex-officer's eye for how agencies actually lean on private companies, informally and deniably. Jones asks what the documents prove and what they only suggest. The Twitter Files remain contested territory, celebrated as exposure and dismissed as selection; Kiriakou's reading is one insider's. The episode's value is the reader as much as the text: a man the CIA prosecuted explaining, from experience, how the relationship between spies and platforms really works.
podcast-tuckercarlson-K_2_7fxyIEI:
Tucker Carlson's crew followed the world's deadliest illegal migration route and reports what they found in this episode. The trail runs through the Darien Gap, the jungle between Colombia and Panama crossed by hundreds of thousands. Their full report is a harrowing piece of field journalism.

The team describes the robbers, rivers, and bodies that mark the route. They interview migrants about why they risk the journey and who profits from it. Carlson frames the trek as a failure of policy on several continents. Sober and compassionate viewers get an unflinching look at a road of suffering.
the-story-of-mattie-j-jackson-her-parent:
Mattie J. Jackson's true story, written and arranged by Dr. L. S. Thompson from Mattie's own telling and printed at Lawrence, Massachusetts, in 1866, recounts her parentage, eighteen years in slavery, incidents during the war, and her escape. She begins with ancestors transported from Africa when the slave trade flourished, explaining that enslaved progenitors had no means of keeping dates.

Her great grandfather was captured in Africa and enslaved in New York under a master named Jackson. Her grandfather, born enslaved in the same state, was emancipated and rewarded with property for his honesty, and hoped to manage his own affairs. A white decoyer then persuaded him to go as a partner to Missouri, and on the schooner voyage to St. Charles he was seized with fever and left unconscious, the first turn in the family's renewed sorrow.
